title: Strings in C++: std::string, cin and getline

visuals.title: The word HELLO is a row of characters (shown as ASCII codes)
Match each string tool to what it does

pairs.meaning: Reads ONE word (stops at a space)
Reads the whole line including spaces
Throws away the leftover Enter before getline
Joins two strings into a new one
A C-style string: fixed size, needs room for the \0 at the end

goal: After this you can declare and fill a std::string, read a word or a whole line, avoid the leftover-newline trap, find the length, look at single characters and join strings with +.
warmup: Your name, your roll number and your address are all text. On a hostel form you write them in boxes. Old-style C boxes (char arrays) have a fixed number of squares: if your name is longer than the boxes, there is trouble. C++ gives you a magic form where the line stretches to fit whatever you write. That is the string class.
definition: A string is a sequence of characters, that is, text. C++ has two kinds. A C-string is a char array that ends with a hidden \0 (null) character and has a fixed size. The std::string class (header <string>) is easier: it grows automatically, can be copied with =, joined with + and compared with ==. In this course we mainly use std::string. Every character has a number called its ASCII code (A is 65, a is 97, 0 is 48).
howItWorks: DECLARE: string s; makes an empty string, string s = "Hello"; fills it. READ: cin >> s reads only ONE word, because it stops at the first space. To read a whole line such as a full name, use getline(cin, s). THE TRAP: after cin >> age; the Enter key you pressed is still waiting in the input. A getline right after it reads that empty rest of the line and seems to be skipped. The cure is cin.ignore(); between them, which throws that one Enter away. SIZE: s.length() (or s.size()) gives the number of characters. It does NOT count a hidden \0 for std::string. CHARACTERS: s[0] is the first character and s[s.length() - 1] the last. s.at(i) does the same, but checks the index. Indexing outside the string with [] is a bug that the compiler does not catch. Caution: length() has an unsigned type (size_t), so use size_t i in loops and be careful with s.length() - 1 on an empty string. LOOPING: for (size_t i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) visits each character; the visual shows HELLO as a row of boxes, with each character stored as its ASCII code. JOINING: a + b makes a new string. You may write s + "!" or s += "!", but "Hi" + " there" (two plain quoted texts) is not allowed: one side must be a string. C-STRINGS FOR COMPARISON: char name[30] = "Ali"; needs strcpy to assign, strcat to join and strcmp to compare; a std::string just uses =, + and ==.
syntax:
#include <string>

string s;                       // empty string
string name = "Ali";           // with a value
string full = name + " Khan";  // + joins (concatenation)

cin >> s;                       // reads ONE word
getline(cin, s);                // reads a whole line
cin.ignore();                   // remove the leftover Enter (between cin >> and getline)

s.length();  s.size();          // number of characters
s[0];        s.at(0);           // first character
s[s.length() - 1];              // last character

for (size_t i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) {
    cout << s[i];               // visit each character
}

char old[30] = "Ali";           // C-string: fixed size, ends with \0

explanation.text: The string class lives in the <string> header.
Declare a string and give it a value in one line.
+ joins (concatenates) strings. At least one side of + must be a string, not two plain quoted texts.
length() gives the number of characters (size() does the same).
[] reads one character. The first index is 0.
at(1) reads the character at index 1 and checks that the index is valid.

steps.note: first is a string box holding the text Ali.
+ joins strings: Ali, then a space, then Khan. A string grows to fit, nothing overflows.
Ali Khan has 3 + 1 + 4 = 8 characters. The space counts too.
Characters are numbered from 0, so full[0] is A.
full.at(1) is the second character, l. at() does the same as [] but checks the index.

sample.title: cin reads a word, getline reads a line

explanation.text: cin >> reads one word only (stops at a space).
Reading a number leaves the Enter key (a newline) in the input.
Removes that leftover newline. Needed between cin >> and getline.
Reads a whole line, spaces included.

steps.note: Two empty strings and an int box are created.
cin >> reads ONE word and stops at the space or Enter. It reads Hamza. The Enter key stays unread in the input.
cin >> skips the leftover Enter and reads 19. The Enter AFTER 19 is still waiting in the input.
ignore() throws away that one leftover newline, so the next getline starts on the real line.
getline reads the WHOLE line including spaces, up to the Enter.
Done. Without cin.ignore(), getline would have read the empty rest of the age line and full would be empty.

mistakes.error: No compiler error. cin >> age leaves the Enter in the input, so getline reads an empty line at once and full stays empty.

mistakes.wrong:
string name;
cin >> name;      // user types: Hamza Ali Khan
mistakes.error: No compiler error, but name holds only Hamza. cin >> stops at the first space; the rest stays in the input. Use getline for text with spaces.
g++ gives: error: invalid operands of types 'const char [3]' and 'const char [7]' to binary 'operator+'. Two plain quoted texts cannot be added; make at least one side a string.
g++ gives: error: conversion from 'char' to non-scalar type 'std::string' requested. Single quotes make a char, double quotes make text.

mistakes.wrong:
string s = "Ali";
cout << s[10];   // outside the string
mistakes.error: No compiler error. Reading past the end gives an unpredictable value or a crash. Always keep the index below s.length().

examTips: State the difference: cin >> reads one word, getline reads the whole line. Mention cin.ignore() whenever a getline follows a cin >> number.
Indexes start at 0, the last index is length() - 1. A string of 8 characters has indexes 0 to 7.
Know the table: C-string vs string: strcpy vs =, strcat vs +, strcmp vs ==, strlen vs length().
Single character = single quotes ('a'), text = double quotes ("a"). Characters have ASCII codes: A is 65, a is 97, 0 is 48.
romanSummary: String text hota hai. C++ mein do tareeqe hain: C-string (char array, aakhir mein \0, fixed size) aur string class (<string>, size khud barhta hai).
cin >> sirf ek word parhta hai; poori line parhne ke liye getline(cin, s) use karein.
cin >> number ke baad getline se pehle cin.ignore() lagana zaroori hai, warna getline skip hota nazar aata hai.
length() se lambai, s[i] ya s.at(i) se ek character, aur + se do strings jorte hain. Index 0 se shuru hota hai.
